newsitem.title: GERMANY: German metal employers seek five-year pay freeze.
newsitem.headline: German metal employers seek five-year pay freeze.

text.p: Germany's metal and engineering employers federation, currently engaged in a bitter dispute with workers over wage and labour costs, said on Wednesday it would be seeking a five-year wage freeze in the sector.
"There can be no further increase in labour costs," Werner Stumpfe, head of the Gesamtmetall employers federation, told a news briefing in Berlin.

He also warned union leaders, who have organised mass protests by workers in the industry against proposed cuts to sick payments and other benefits, that further industrial action could "destroy the gradual upturn in the sector".
IG Metall, Germany's largest trade union with a membership approaching three million, has warned that all-out strikes are possible next year if a solution to the dispute is not found.

The trade union has said it would accept a 1997 pay increase in line with inflation, but only if accompanied by expenditure by employers on measures to protect job levels in the metal and engineering industries.

Gesamtmetall on the other hand wants a "cost-neutral" 1997 wage round, which would imply cost cut-backs of some form if even a small wage increase was agreed. It has slated holiday and Christmas bonuses in the sector as possible targets.
But Stumpfe said that it was the issue of sick pay, which a new law allows employs to reduce by 20 percent, where there was most disagreement.
"We have never had so tough a package as this one to negotiate," he said.

Talks between union and Gesamtmetall negotiators aimed at finding a natiomal agreement on sick pay and wages collapsed in October, leaving regional wage committees across Germany with the task of hammering out local deals.
The two sides are due to meet in the steel-making region of North-Rhine Westphalia, the largest single employer in the industry, to discuss a possible deal next Monday.

The meeting comes as the temperature of the debate over labour costs faced by German companies was sent rising by a Bundesbank report earlier this week suggesting that wage moderation this year would help companies to improved profits.

Gesamtmetall on Tuesday denied that such a prognosis could be applied to the metal and engineering sector, where it said unit wage costs had risen 6.5 percent above last year's level in the first eight months of the year.
It said this would mean that profits in the sector would in fact fall by 10 percent this year.

IG Metall on Wednesday refuted the Gesamtmetall statement, arguing that wage costs had only risen 5.5 percent compared to a productivity gain of 6.8 percent, thus leaving room for a small profit increase in the industry.
